newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebel stand-off ends, dying leader to travel.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebel stand-off ends, dying leader to travel.

text.p: Mexico's government and Zapatista rebels ended a tense stand-off on Wednesday after rebels won a concession to send a dying woman leader to the capital to attend an Indian forum.

Rebel leader Subcommander Marcos announced Commander Romana's trip, the first time a Zapatista leader has been able to leave the southeastern state of Chiapas since the uprising began in January 1994.
He said it was the once-powerful Totzil woman's "dying wish" to attend the forum as a Zapatista representative. She has terminal cancer, her colleagues said.
The government of President Ernesto Zedillo had threatened to arrest any Zapatista leaders who sought to attend the National Indigenous Congress unless they laid down their arms.

Though the government has carried out on-and-off peace talks for more than a year with the rebels, it has sought to contain the uprising in Chiapas and carefully resisted any efforts by the Zapatistas to claim national scope.

After rebel leaders appeared dead set on attending the forum, negotiations dragged on for three days between rebels in their stronghold of La Realidad and a congressional peace mediating body that reported back to the government.

Late on Tuesday, the mediators flew back to Mexico City when talks seemed on the point of collapse, and the government insisted afterward the negotiations were about ending the 2-1/2 year-old conflict, not safe passes out of Chiapas.

It was not immediately clear what concessions the Zapatista rebels may have given the mediators in return for winning agreement for Ramona to travel. Marcos insisted the rebels had never sought the government's permission.
The charismatic leader, who is fond of theatrical gestures, milked the occasion in style.

After announcing the rebels were sending their "most belligerent, most aggressive, most war-like" delegation, he produced the infirm Ramona, who was carried onto a makeshift stage by colleagues, wearing the rebels' trademark ski-mask.
Ramona has been reported dead many times since she was diagnosed with terminal cancer two years ago, and has not been seen in public since the early days of the conflict.
"Nevermore a Federal District (Mexico City) without us," Marcos boomed, playing on the slogan of the four-day Indian congress in the capital, "Nevermore a Mexico without us."

Ramona was due to fly to Mexico City on Thursday. It was not clear whether she would get medical treatment, but her visit was sure to raise the profile of the forum that started on Tuesday in somewhat lackluster style.

Many of Mexico's 8-million-strong Indian community say their struggle for recognition in the country has been bolstered by the Zapatista uprising for democracy and Indian rights since 1994. Some see the rebels as heroes.
